data.title: UraniumX Announces Flow-Through Private Placement
data.description:
VANCOUVER, BC / ACCESS Newswire / November 27, 2026 / UraniumX Discovery Corp. (CSE:STMN)(OTCQB:STMXF)(FSE:Q7S) (the "Company" or "UraniumX") is pleased to announce a non-brokered private placement of up to 36,363,636 flow-through shares at a price of $0.055 per FT Share for aggregate gross proceeds of up to $2,000,000 (each a "FT Share") (the "Offering"). No warrants will be issued to subscribers in connection with the Offering. The Company may increase the size of the Offering to accommodate additional demand.

The FT Shares will qualify as "flow-through shares" within the meaning of subsection 66(15) of the Income Tax Act (Canada). The Company intends to use the gross proceeds from the sale of FT Shares to incur eligible" Canadian exploration expenses" that qualify as "flow-through critical mineral mining expenditures" within the meaning of subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act (Canada), which will be renounced to the subscribers in an amount not less than the subscription price of the FT Shares, with an effective date no later than December 31, 2026 and to incur such expenses on or before December 31, 2027.

Proceeds will fund the Company's ongoing exploration activities at Murphy Lake.

Closing of the Offering is subject to receipt of all necessary corporate and regulatory approvals, including the approval of the Canadian Securities Exchange. All securities issued under the Offering will be subject to a statutory hold period of four months and one day from the date of issuance.

The Company may pay finder's fees to eligible persons in connection with the Offering, in accordance with the policies of the Canadian Securities Exchange.

About UraniumX Discovery Corp.

UraniumX Discovery Corp. is a Canadian-based junior uranium exploration company focused on advancing uranium properties in Saskatchewan's Athabasca Basin, one of Canada's most active uranium districts. The Company's flagship Murphy Lake Uranium Property is located in the northeastern Athabasca Basin, where UraniumX is earning up to a 70% interest through an option agreement with F4 Uranium Corp. UraniumX additionally holds 100% interests in the Zoo Bay and NeoCore uranium properties, and is advancing a project generator approach across its broader portfolio by optioning non-core assets while retaining royalties and equity, allowing the Company to concentrate exploration capital on Murphy Lake.

On Behalf of UraniumX Discovery Corp.

Esen Boldkhuu, CEO

Contact:

UraniumX Discovery Corp.
Esen Boldkhuu, CEO
Email: info@uraniumx.ca
Telephone: (604) 377-8994
Website: www.uraniumx.ca

Forward Looking Statements

This news release contains "forward looking information" and "forward looking statements" within the meaning of applicable Canadian securities laws (collectively, "forward looking statements"). All statements, other than statements of historical fact, included herein are forward looking statements. Forward looking statements in this release include, but are not limited to, statements regarding the Offering, the renunciation of exploration expenses, and the Company's future plans, objectives, and exploration activities.

Forward looking statements are based on reasonable assumptions, estimates, and opinions of management as of the date hereof and are subject to known and unknown risks, uncertainties, and other factors that may cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied by such forward looking statements. These factors include, but are not limited to, the Company's inability to complete the Offering on the terms described herein or at all, fluctuations in market conditions, volatility in equity and capital markets, risks inherent in mineral exploration and development, environmental risks, reliance on key personnel, regulatory approvals, and changes in laws and regulations.

data.title: I hate that Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia, but I love what it's done for my 401(k). Am I a hypocrite?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

Doing nothing and maintaining an even temperament is often the work of gods

Jensen Huang, who on Monday returned as CEO of Nvidia. (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I was paralyzed during the market downturn, so I have a question in the event that this bounce - led by the shocking and, in my opinion, unwelcome news that Jensen Huang has returned as Nvidia's (NVDA) CEO - does not last. No comment on that, as it happens, even though I have my opinions, like most people do.

I'm writing to you about my own strategy, not to pass judgment on other people's corporate decisions. During a market downturn, is it better for me to draw down cash from CDs for the next year or two rather than taking money from my equities and annuities at a loss? Where are the safe havens? I don't want to eat into my retirement savings.

Planning Ahead

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: America is divided into two countries - Trump's pro-billionaires and Mamdani's anti-billionaires

Being paralyzed during the recent volatility in the market is not exactly a bad thing.

Dear Planning,

It's fair to say that many people were surprised by Jensen Huang's return on Monday - and you are not alone in having strong opinions on that.

Some of the same people who cried foul over the fall in their 401(k)s and IRAs may well be rolling their eyes over the return of Huang to the helm of Nvidia, which now appears to be the cornerstone of the AI revolution, mostly due to its multibillion-dollar microchip business and proprietary software ecosystem. Indeed, the stock gave up some of Monday's gains on Tuesday as investors turned their attention to regulatory concerns about the export of U.S. microchips to China and elsewhere. Huang was effectively fired (he officially resigned) from the company a couple of weeks ago over his reported affairs with two employees, as well as one with a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese spy.

Commentators have questioned whether President Donald Trump overlooked the potential and alleged national-security threat by calling for Huang's return to Nvidia NVDA, thereby signaling that the company is too big to fail. Others bemoaned the decision by the company's board and wondered what the role of such boards is, if not to uphold professional, legal and personal standards. While low-wage American workers have been fired over bathroom breaks, skeptics may wonder if rules of conduct only apply to nonbillionaires.

It's OK to have joys and concerns about the billionaire class and your 401(k), even if the answers conflict with each other.

And, honestly, being paralyzed during the recent volatility in the market is not exactly a bad thing, either. Doing nothing and maintaining an even temperament is often the work of gods. Some people panic and sell, or move into real estate, bonds, or gold, and constantly check their 401(k) while getting upset over paper losses. Yet short-term swings won't have a big impact if they aren't about to retire or haven't just retired - especially if they have cash alternatives. How many times a day or week did you check your 401(k) when the market was on the rise? I'm guessing not a lot.

I sympathize with your urge to check. According to a 2026 report by the Investment Company Institute (ICI), a global trade association representing regulated funds and their shareholders, 81% of mutual fund-owning U.S. households hold stock funds - most of them inside workplace retirement plans. Because broad stock and index funds are heavily weighted toward mega-cap AI leaders like Nvidia, a significant share of American households are naturally exposed to those stocks. "Mutual funds play a key role in their households' balance sheets," the researchers wrote.

But back to the other questions in your letter: Yes, drawing from CDs and relying on annuity income can be a smart move. That assumes you don't have required minimum distributions from a traditional retirement account and your CDs have reached the end of their term. If you paid extra for a guaranteed lifetime income rider on your annuities - locking in an income stream if markets plummet or your account balance falls to zero - that will protect you during a correction, while fixed annuities aren't tied to the market's fortunes at all. Having cash alternatives helps you avoid "sequence-of-returns risk," where poor market performance in the early years of retirement puts pressure on a portfolio you're drawing from.

Don't miss: 'Nvidia's turmoil has me spooked': Is it time to sell my stocks and buy real estate?

Timing the market vs. managing risk

Darius Dale, founder and CEO of 42 Macro, a macroeconomic research and systematic risk-management firm, predicts that markets will return to a "risk-on market regime," where investors favor higher risk assets over safe havens, within a couple of months. "Hope is not an effective risk-management process," he says. "Positioning for the market regime helps investors avoid fear of missing out (FOMO) and fear of more losses (FOML). FOMO causes investors to buy cycle tops, and FOML causes investors to sell cycle lows. These are the two worst things any investor can do to their financial well-being."

As for your curiosity about safe havens, I can understand why you would consider them after such a volatile week, especially with lingering questions about the stock market's heavy dependence on AI. The right mix depends on your risk tolerance and, as Dale suggested, your expectations about the economic outlook, especially if you want to factor in how reliant the economy is becoming on AI. There are many paths to take. Andrew Clinton, CEO of Clinton Investment Management, suggests municipal bonds as a haven during a correction.

I can understand why you would look for safe havens, especially with lingering questions about the market's heavy dependence on AI.

Municipal bonds are, for the record, more appropriate for investors in higher tax brackets with money held in taxable accounts who live in high-tax states, and for retirees prioritizing cash flow and capital preservation. "Municipal bonds offer attractive tax-adjusted carry and stable underlying asset-class credit quality for investors seeking durable cash flows amidst equity-market volatility," he says. "Current municipal bond yields remain near the most attractive levels in decades."

Clinton also has a rosier outlook on the underlying strength of the U.S. economy than, perhaps, many folks. "Credit fundamentals remain strong, with default rates representing only a fraction of corporate default rates," he says. "Municipal issuers provide essential services such as airports, utilities and toll roads, generating durable cash flows with limited exposure to corporate earnings volatility. If inflation moderates and rates decline, municipals offer the potential for both attractive income and capital appreciation."

For other safe havens, consider shorter-duration bonds, mutual funds and exchange-traded funds that invest in bonds with maturities of less than five years, as well as Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS) backed by the U.S. Treasury to guard against rising prices. Give a thought to value-oriented and defensive sectors, including consumer-staples, utilities and healthcare stocks, for retired investors who seek stability over higher returns. Your lifestyle, the balances in your retirement accounts, your goals, your financial profile - whether you have a mortgage, debt or long-term-care insurance - and your views on AI all play a role.

Pausing during a storm does not mean you suffer from paralysis, and you don't have to like the news in order to plan around it.

Your letter attests to that.

Related: Is Social Security a Ponzi scheme? No. Don't get carried away with 1930s-era prophecies of doom.

data.title: Clearing out my parents' house was a legal nightmare. How can I downsize without putting my kids through the same ordeal?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

Some countercultural advice this Black Friday: stop buying stuff, plus other rules for downsizing

"Legal fees ended up eating up half the value of my parents' estate." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I have recently read and heard a lot about the recommendation for seniors to take an active role in managing their estates - specifically by downsizing, in addition to having the wills and estate plans you have advised for years. Downsizing means going through all the "stuff" accumulated over the years and weeding out the treasures and clutter we no longer use, need or want.

While many seniors do this when they move into a retirement community, plenty of us stay put in our homes for decades. My parents lived in their home from 1950 to 2020. They believed their children would enjoy going through their belongings and reminiscing after they passed, but the reality was quite different and a massive hassle.

None of us lived nearby, we argued over what to do with 70 years' worth of possessions, and eventually, lawyers and the courts got involved. Legal fees ate up half the value of my parents' estate. Downsizing is difficult because of sentimental attachments, the sheer physical energy it requires and the challenge of knowing what is valuable versus what to let go of.

In my own downsizing efforts, I've avoided the hassle of online listings, garage sales or hiring estate experts, opting instead to give things to neighbors, donate them to Goodwill or toss them. What advice can you share for seniors who have too much stuff, feel overwhelmed by the process and want to spare their families what mine went through?

Aging Downsizer

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: My husband wants to sell our $1.5 million home and downsize. But this is where we raised our kids - and I can't bear to leave.

You will be surprised how quickly you forget about items once they're gone.

Dear Downsizer,

Sticky notes on furniture is no substitute for a proper will.

Your experience clearing out your parents' home is a cautionary tale. Hiring lawyers can cost a fortune and escalate disagreements that could be better resolved with a mediator. When it comes to family, going to court should be the very last resort. Aging parents can start giving away their valuable items to their children in an effort to prevent arguments later on, or put in place a system for choosing them, such as labeling items or drawing straws and allowing each child to choose an item in rotation.

Be aware that giving away expensive antiques, jewelry, or furniture during your lifetime with a combined value exceeding $19,000 per recipient in a single calendar year will require you to file a gift-tax return (IRS Form 709), even though you won't actually owe taxes unless you exceed the multi-million-dollar lifetime exemption. An important sticky note for your estate plans: Naming a third party as executor, and giving them authority in your will to sell any items your children can't agree upon within, say, 30 days, will help keep any family disputes out of court.

Without further ado - and I hope this helps you - here are some tips for clearing your house:

5 rules of downsizing

(1) Be tough. Without throwing out something valuable like an antique, a letter from a loved one or a wedding photo album that can never be replaced, you have to be ruthless when downsizing. And while the struggle is real, you need to avoid engaging in it every time you open a box. Your memories are not packed away in an attic or basement. They are in your mind and they are in your heart.

(2) Think digital. After you have had the hard conversations with your children about what they want or what they don't want, you can take photos of a treasured childhood toy before donating it or throwing it in the garbage. And a Kindle or the Apple Books app takes up less space than thousands of physical books.You can always put your favorite memories on social media or put them in a shared online folder so family members have access to them.

(3) Take it easy. The emotional labor is as challenging as the physical labor. You are, after all, sifting through your memories, which will bring up good and possibly also bad or painful moments. Take your time. You acquired these belongings over a lifetime, so why would you put yourself through the onerous task of dismantling your life in a week or a month? Commit to one big garbage bag per day. If you do two per day, take Sunday off.

(4) Out of sight, out of mind. You will be surprised how quickly you forget about items once they're gone. Anyone who has moved house and lived without their belongings for a period of time will have experienced this. Our stuff becomes part of our identity. Sure, everyone has their own treasures - a piece of artwork that won't take up too much space on a wall - but you may be surprised how quickly you forget about items once they're out of sight.

The emotional labor is often as challenging as the physical labor.

(5) Stop buying. Some countercultural advice this Black Friday - stop buying stuff that replaces the stuff you threw out. Perhaps it's that 2026 holiday sweater that looks so enticing online, even when we have a closet full of old sweaters crying out to be worn. We all love a bargain, and Black Friday and Cyber Monday tempt us to spend, spend, spend (analysts forecast spending nearing $30 billion for both "consumer holidays" this year). Don't replace the stuff you throw out.

Make spring cleaning an annual or semiannual event. As writer Evelyn Richards noted in this personal reflection in Country Living Magazine about downsizing from a three-bedroom house to a one-bedroom apartment: "Decluttering isn't just about tidying up your home; it's also about nurturing your mental well-being. When you clear out the excess and organize your space, you create a serene and stress-free environment."

It feels lighter to walk into a room where everything is in order, she writes. "This kind of order can significantly reduce anxiety and make it easier to relax. When your home is clutter-free, it's like a breath of fresh air, allowing you to focus on what truly matters. Moreover, the process of decluttering itself can be therapeutic. As you sort through items, you make decisions about what to keep and what to let go, which can be incredibly empowering."

I'm resisting buying yet another pair of sneakers this Black Friday because, like you, I have too much stuff. I sometimes wonder how much money I would have saved in my life had I stuck to a black cashmere turtleneck like Apple's late CEO Steve Jobs or a black leather jacket like Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang. You have accumulated a lifetime of memories - and, presumably, a few savvy investments in artwork and furniture - and passing those treasures on to loved ones should be a joy. Still, even the most discerning consumer ends up with clutter.

The ceramic bunny rabbit has got to go.

Related: This is the best Black Friday purchase I ever made

data.title: Southwest Heritage Bank Announces Acquisition Agreement with Peak Credit Union
data.description:
SCOTTSDALE, AZ / ACCESS Newswire / November 27, 2026 / Southwest Heritage Bank, together with the bank's parent company, Bancorp 34, Inc. (OTCID:BCTF), today announced a definitive agreement for Peak Credit Union ("Peak") to acquire Southwest Heritage Bank. Under the agreement, Peak would acquire substantially all of Southwest Heritage Bank's assets and assume substantially all of its liabilities in an all-cash transaction.

The transaction was unanimously approved by the boards of directors of Peak Credit Union, Southwest Heritage Bank, and Bancorp 34, Inc. The acquisition is subject to customary regulatory and stockholder approvals and is expected to be completed in the second half of 2027. Following completion of the transaction, Southwest Heritage Bank and Bancorp 34, Inc. will dissolve and the remaining assets will be distributed to the stockholders of Bancorp 34, Inc. Subject to the terms of the agreement, stockholders are expected to receive an estimated $20.67 to $22.18 per share for an aggregate transaction value of $ 159 million to $171 million.

Peak intends to retain members of Southwest Heritage Bank's executive leadership team in senior roles within the combined organization, drawing on their expertise and experience to guide a successful integration and contribute to the credit union's long-term growth and strategic direction. In particular, Southwest Heritage Bank President Paul Tees will be responsible for leading commercial banking across the combined organization, bringing the bank's commercial lending expertise and local-market-led, relationship focused approach to Peak's broader network.

Peak also intends to retain all Southwest Heritage Bank employees immediately upon closing, subject to ordinary business and individual circumstances, to ensure continuity of service and the successful integration of the organizations' systems and processes.

Until the transaction closes, both organizations will continue to operate independently, and there is nothing customers or members need to do.

D.A. Davidson & Co. served as financial advisor and Otteson Shapiro LLP served as legal counsel to Bancorp 34, Inc. and Southwest Heritage Bank. McQueen Financial Advisors served as financial advisor and Luse Gorman, PC served as legal counsel to Peak Credit Union.

Investor Contact: Kevin Vaughn, CFO, 623-334-6064. BCTF@swhb.com

About Bancorp 34, Inc.

Bancorp 34, Inc. is the holding company for Southwest Heritage Bank. The bank's headquarters are located at 8777 East Hartford Drive, Suite 100, Scottsdale, Arizona 85255. In addition, the bank operates seven full-service community bank branches, two in Maricopa County, Arizona, in the cities of Scottsdale and Gilbert; three in Pima County, Arizona, in the cities of Tucson and Green Valley; one branch in Otero County, New Mexico in the city of Alamogordo; and one branch in Dona Ana County New Mexico, in the city of Las Cruces.

About Peak Credit Union

About Peak Credit Union: Peak Credit Union is a member-owned, not-for-profit financial cooperative serving more than 250,000 members through 35 branches across Washington and Oregon and digital banking services. Formed from the combination of TwinStar Credit Union and Northwest Community Credit Union, Peak brings a longstanding commitment to financial education, accessible financial services and community well-being. Through the PeakCU Foundation, Peak supports local initiatives including classroom grants, scholarships and financial education. Federally insured by NCUA. Equal Housing Opportunity. Learn more at peakcu.org.
